question.title: Cloud Spanner Configuration
question.scenario: A company is deploying Cloud Spanner for their globally distributed inventory system. They need to decide between regional and multi-region configurations.
question.question-text: What is the primary benefit of a Cloud Spanner multi-region configuration over a regional configuration?

choices.choice: Simpler schema design requirements
Lower latency for all read operations
Higher availability SLA and survives regional outages
Reduced cost compared to regional

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Multi-region Spanner replicates data across multiple regions, offering a 99.999% SLA versus 99.99% for regional — focus on the availability and fault-tolerance benefit.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Cloud Spanner multi-region configurations replicate data across several regions, delivering a 99.999% (five nines) availability SLA and the ability to survive an entire regional outage without data loss. Regional configurations offer 99.99% availability at lower cost but cannot tolerate a full region failure. Multi-region does not simplify schema design or reduce cost; in fact it costs roughly 3x more. Read latency for stale reads can improve via local replicas, but write latency increases due to cross-region consensus.

ul.li: Multi-region write latency is higher because Spanner must achieve quorum across geographically distant replicas before committing a transaction.
Stale reads (bounded staleness or exact staleness) can be served from the nearest replica, reducing read latency, but strong reads still route to the leader region.
Multi-region configurations cost approximately 3x a comparable single-region setup due to the extra replica storage and cross-region network traffic.
Google offers predefined multi-region configurations (e.g., nam-eur-asia1) and allows custom placements for specific compliance or latency requirements.

question.title: AlloyDB Architecture
question.scenario: An architect is designing a system using AlloyDB and needs to understand how to scale read capacity independently from the primary instance.
question.question-text: How does AlloyDB enable scaling read capacity without affecting the primary instance?

choices.choice: Memory-cached read replicas only
Cross-region read replicas with separate storage
Read pool instances that share storage with the primary
Automatic read query routing to BigQuery

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: AlloyDB's disaggregated architecture means read pool nodes connect to the same distributed storage layer as the primary, so adding read capacity requires no data duplication.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: AlloyDB separates compute from storage. Read pool instances are additional compute nodes that share the same distributed storage layer as the primary, so they see the latest committed data without asynchronous replication lag or storage duplication. This lets you spin up or tear down read capacity in minutes. Memory-only caching would lose data on restart, cross-region replicas with separate storage introduce replication lag and double storage cost, and routing to BigQuery adds latency and is not suitable for OLTP reads.

ul.li: Read pool instances can be provisioned or removed in minutes because they attach to existing storage rather than copying data, eliminating the bootstrap time of traditional replicas.
The shared storage layer replicates data synchronously across zones for durability, so all read pool nodes inherit the same regional resilience as the primary.
Applications connect to a single read pool endpoint that load-balances across all read pool nodes, simplifying connection management and avoiding application-side routing logic.
Unlike Cloud SQL read replicas, AlloyDB read pool instances do not maintain a separate WAL stream, reducing network overhead and ensuring near-zero read lag.

question.title: Cloud SQL Connection Methods
question.scenario: A developer needs to connect their application running on Google Kubernetes Engine to a Cloud SQL instance securely without managing SSL certificates.
question.question-text: What is the recommended method for connecting GKE workloads to Cloud SQL securely?

choices.choice: Direct TCP connection over VPC
Cloud SQL Auth Proxy
Public IP with firewall rules
SSH tunnel through a bastion host

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Consider the lightweight proxy that handles IAM-based authentication and TLS encryption to Cloud SQL automatically, eliminating the need to manage SSL certificates or IP allowlists.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: The Cloud SQL Auth Proxy is Google's recommended connector for GKE-to-Cloud SQL communication. It runs as a sidecar container in each pod, uses IAM credentials for authentication, and encrypts the connection with TLS — all without requiring you to manage certificates, configure authorized networks, or expose a public IP. Direct VPC TCP connections are possible with Private IP but require VPC peering setup. Public IP with firewall rules is less secure and harder to maintain. SSH tunnels add operational overhead and latency.

ul.li: The Auth Proxy supports IAM database authentication, which maps IAM principals to database users, enabling centralized access control and eliminating the need for static database passwords.
In GKE, the proxy is typically deployed as a sidecar container that listens on localhost, so the application connects to 127.0.0.1 on the configured port and the proxy handles all upstream security.
Private IP connections via VPC peering are also secure and avoid the public internet, but they require VPC network configuration and do not provide IAM-based per-user authentication by default.
Public IP access requires maintaining authorized network CIDR ranges and rotating SSL certificates, making it operationally expensive compared to the Auth Proxy's automatic handling.

question.title: Cloud SQL Read Replicas
question.scenario: An application has high read traffic that overwhelms the primary Cloud SQL instance. The team wants to distribute read load while keeping the primary for writes.
question.question-text: Which Cloud SQL feature allows distributing read traffic across multiple instances?

choices.choice: Query insights
High availability configuration
Read replicas
Connection pooling

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Think about the Cloud SQL feature that creates asynchronous copies of the primary instance specifically to offload read queries and scale read throughput horizontally.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Cloud SQL read replicas are asynchronous copies of the primary that handle read queries, distributing read traffic and reducing load on the primary. Applications must direct reads to replica endpoints and writes to the primary. Query insights is a monitoring tool, not a scaling feature. HA configuration provides failover redundancy but does not serve read traffic. Connection pooling helps manage connection counts but does not add read capacity.

ul.li: Cloud SQL supports up to 10 read replicas per primary instance, and replicas can be placed in different zones or even cross-region for lower read latency in other geographies.
Replication is asynchronous, so replicas may lag the primary by seconds under heavy write load; applications must tolerate eventual consistency for replica reads.
Cross-region read replicas can be promoted to standalone primary instances for disaster recovery, though promotion severs the replication link permanently.
Read replicas do not participate in HA failover — they are separate from the HA standby instance and serve a different purpose (read scaling vs. write availability).

question.title: Cloud Spanner Schema Design
question.scenario: A team designing a Cloud Spanner schema for an order management system needs to store orders and order items. They want to optimize for queries that fetch an order with all its items.
question.question-text: Which Cloud Spanner schema design pattern optimizes parent-child data retrieval?

choices.choice: Interleaved tables with parent-child relationship
Separate tables with foreign key joins
Denormalized single table with repeated fields
Multiple databases with cross-database queries

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Spanner has a unique schema feature that physically co-locates child rows with their parent row on the same split, making parent-child reads a single local operation.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Cloud Spanner's interleaved tables store child rows physically adjacent to their parent row within the same storage split. For an order management system, interleaving OrderItems under Orders means fetching an order and all its items reads contiguous storage, minimizing the number of splits accessed and reducing latency. Foreign key joins across non-interleaved tables may span multiple splits, increasing latency. Denormalization wastes storage and complicates updates. Spanner does not support cross-database queries.

ul.li: Interleaving is declared with the INTERLEAVE IN PARENT clause in DDL; child rows must include the parent's primary key columns as a prefix of their own primary key.
Interleaved tables share the same split as their parent, so a single read or transaction on a parent key range accesses all related child rows without cross-split coordination.

Avoid interleaving when parent-child data is rarely queried together or when child tables are very large, because co-location increases the size of individual splits and may trigger more frequent split operations.
ON DELETE CASCADE can be specified on interleaved tables so that deleting a parent row automatically removes all interleaved child rows in the same transaction.

question.title: Firestore Modes
question.scenario: A team is migrating from Datastore to Firestore and needs to understand the differences between Firestore modes.
question.question-text: What is the main difference between Firestore Native mode and Datastore mode?

choices.choice: Datastore mode has higher query throughput than Native mode
Datastore mode supports SQL queries; Native mode does not
Native mode is regional only; Datastore mode is multi-regional
Native mode supports real-time updates and mobile SDKs; Datastore mode is compatible with legacy Datastore APIs

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: The key distinction is feature set: Native mode unlocks real-time listeners and mobile/web SDKs, while Datastore mode preserves backward compatibility with the legacy Cloud Datastore API.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Firestore Native mode delivers the full Firestore experience — real-time listeners, offline persistence, mobile and web SDKs, and the document/collection data model. Datastore mode maintains backward compatibility with Cloud Datastore APIs and client libraries, making it the right choice only when an existing Datastore application must migrate without rewriting data-access code. Neither mode supports SQL; both support strong consistency. Throughput and regional/multi-regional availability are configuration choices, not mode differences.

ul.li: Mode selection is permanent and cannot be changed after the database is created, so the decision must be made during initial provisioning.
Both modes now provide strong consistency for all queries, unlike the original Cloud Datastore which had eventual consistency for non-ancestor queries.
Native mode is recommended for all new applications; Datastore mode should only be chosen when maintaining compatibility with existing Datastore client libraries is a hard requirement.
Datastore mode does not support real-time listeners, mobile/web SDKs, or the collection-group query feature available in Native mode.

question.title: Bigtable Row Key Design
question.scenario: A team is designing a Bigtable schema for storing user activity logs. They need to efficiently query recent activities for a specific user.
question.question-text: What is the recommended row key design for querying user activities by recency?

choices.choice: Timestamp only
Auto-incrementing sequential ID
Random UUID for each activity
User ID combined with reverse timestamp

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: An effective Bigtable row key for this pattern prefixes with the user identifier to group data, then appends a reverse timestamp so the most recent entries sort first in a scan.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Combining user ID with a reverse timestamp (Long.MAX_VALUE minus the actual timestamp) as the row key groups all of a user's activities together in Bigtable's lexicographically sorted key space and ensures the most recent entries appear first in a row range scan. Timestamp-only keys create write hotspots on a single node. Auto-incrementing IDs cause the same hotspot problem. Random UUIDs distribute writes evenly but make per-user queries impossible without a full table scan.

ul.li: Monotonically increasing keys (plain timestamps, sequential IDs) concentrate all writes on one tablet server, creating a hotspot that limits throughput to a single node's capacity.
Row key design should reflect the most common access pattern: if queries always filter by user then sort by time, the key should encode that hierarchy (user first, time second).
Field promotion — adding query-predicate fields into the row key — is a core Bigtable design principle because Bigtable has no secondary indexes; all efficient lookups must be row key prefix scans.
For high-cardinality users, the user ID prefix naturally distributes writes across tablets; for low-cardinality groupings, consider salting the key with a hash prefix to avoid hotspots.

question.title: Bigtable Cluster Configuration
question.scenario: A company needs Bigtable to serve traffic from multiple regions with high availability and the ability to survive a regional outage.
question.question-text: How should Bigtable be configured for multi-region high availability?

choices.choice: Create a Bigtable instance with clusters in multiple regions using replication
Deploy separate Bigtable instances and sync data with Dataflow
Use Cloud Spanner instead as Bigtable does not support multi-region
Configure cross-region backup and restore procedures

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Bigtable natively supports multi-cluster replication within a single instance, automatically syncing data between clusters placed in different regions.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Bigtable supports adding multiple clusters to a single instance, with each cluster in a different region. Replication between clusters is automatic and eventually consistent, typically converging within seconds. Applications can use app profiles to route traffic to the nearest cluster or fail over transparently during regional outages. Deploying separate instances with Dataflow sync is complex and fragile. Spanner is a different product for different workloads. Cross-region backup/restore has high RPO and does not provide continuous availability.

ul.li: Replication is eventually consistent with typical convergence lag under one minute; last-writer-wins conflict resolution applies when the same cell is written concurrently in different clusters.

App profiles control routing: multi-cluster routing sends traffic to the nearest healthy cluster, single-cluster routing pins to one cluster, and cluster group routing limits traffic to a subset of clusters.
Each cluster is billed independently for its node-hours and storage; inter-cluster replication network traffic is also billed, so multi-region costs scale with both cluster count and write volume.
You can add or remove clusters from a running instance without downtime; Bigtable automatically rebalances data to new clusters and drains removed clusters gracefully.

question.title: Bigtable vs Firestore
question.scenario: A team is choosing between Bigtable and Firestore for a new application that will store structured data with moderate query complexity.
question.question-text: When should you choose Firestore over Bigtable?

choices.choice: When you need document queries, real-time sync, and automatic scaling from zero
When you need to store petabytes of time-series data
When you need HBase API compatibility
When consistent sub-10ms latency is critical

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Firestore is the right pick when you need flexible document queries, real-time synchronization, mobile/web SDKs, and the ability to scale to zero during idle periods.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Choose Firestore when your application needs flexible document-model queries, real-time synchronization across clients, offline support, and serverless scaling that includes scaling to zero cost during inactivity. Choose Bigtable for analytics-scale workloads: petabytes of time-series or event data, consistent sub-10ms latency at high throughput, and HBase API compatibility. Bigtable requires at least one always-on node, making it cost-prohibitive for low-traffic or bursty apps where Firestore's pay-per-operation model excels.

ul.li: Firestore charges per document operation (read, write, delete) plus storage, so idle apps pay nearly nothing; Bigtable charges per node-hour with a minimum of one node regardless of traffic.
Bigtable supports only single-row transactions with no secondary indexes, while Firestore supports multi-document ACID transactions and automatic single-field indexes with optional composite indexes.
Firestore provides real-time listeners and offline persistence through client SDKs; Bigtable has no built-in sync or offline capability and is accessed via server-side HBase or gRPC APIs.

For workloads between 1 TB and 10 TB with moderate query complexity, the decision often hinges on access pattern: document lookups with real-time sync favor Firestore, while sequential scan and time-range queries favor Bigtable.

question.title: Firestore Indexes
question.scenario: A developer receives an error when running a Firestore query that filters on multiple fields.
question.question-text: Why might a Firestore query with multiple field filters fail?

choices.choice: Authentication is required for multi-field queries
Firestore does not support queries with multiple filters
A composite index must be created for queries with multiple field filters
The fields must be in the same document collection

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Firestore automatically indexes each field individually, but queries filtering on multiple fields require an explicitly created composite index covering those fields.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Firestore creates single-field indexes automatically for every field in every document, but queries that filter or sort on multiple fields require a composite index that must be created explicitly. When a query needs a missing composite index, Firestore returns an error message that includes a direct link to the Cloud Console to create the required index. Authentication is not related to index availability, Firestore does support multi-field queries (with the right index), and fields must be in the queried collection but that is not the cause of the error.

ul.li: Composite indexes can be created via the Firebase Console, the gcloud CLI, or declaratively in a firestore.indexes.json file deployed with firebase deploy --only firestore:indexes.

Each composite index incurs storage overhead and adds write latency because Firestore must update the index entry on every write to an indexed field; limit composite indexes to queries you actually run.
Firestore enforces a maximum of 200 composite indexes per database; exceeding this limit requires consolidating query patterns or restructuring the data model.
Collection-group queries (querying across all subcollections with the same name) also require a composite index with collection-group scope, which must be enabled explicitly.

question.title: Bigtable Garbage Collection
question.scenario: A team stores time-series data in Bigtable and needs to automatically delete data older than 30 days to control costs.
question.question-text: How can Bigtable automatically remove old data based on age?

choices.choice: Create a separate table for each day and drop old tables
Schedule Cloud Functions to delete old rows
Configure garbage collection policies on column families
Use TTL settings on individual cells

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Bigtable uses garbage collection (GC) policies defined at the column family level to automatically expire cells by age or version count during background compaction.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Bigtable garbage collection policies are configured per column family and define when individual cells become eligible for automatic deletion. Policies can be based on cell age (e.g., delete cells older than 30 days) or version count (e.g., keep only the latest 3 versions). GC runs during background compaction, so expired data is removed without manual intervention. Creating separate tables per day is operationally complex, Cloud Functions introduce external scheduling overhead, and Bigtable does not support per-cell TTL settings independent of column family GC policies.

ul.li: GC policies can combine age and version rules using union (delete if either condition is met) or intersection (delete only if both conditions are met) logic for fine-grained retention control.
Expired data may still be returned by reads until the next compaction physically removes the cells; applications should not rely on GC for immediate deletion guarantees.
GC operates at the cell level, not the row level — removing all cells from a row does not delete the row key itself until compaction cleans up the empty row marker.
Different column families within the same table can have different GC policies, allowing hot data (recent metrics) and cold data (historical summaries) to coexist with independent retention rules.

question.title: Cloud Storage Encryption
question.scenario: A financial services company requires that they manage the encryption keys for data stored in Cloud Storage.
question.question-text: Which encryption option allows customers to control encryption keys stored in Cloud KMS?

choices.choice: Google-managed encryption keys
Customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK)
Customer-supplied encryption keys (CSEK)
Client-side encryption

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: CMEK uses encryption keys that you create and manage in Cloud KMS, giving you control over key rotation, access policies, and the ability to revoke access by disabling a key.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK) let you create and manage encryption keys in Cloud Key Management Service (KMS). You control key rotation schedules, set IAM policies on keys, and can revoke data access entirely by disabling or destroying the key. Google-managed keys provide default encryption but give you no control over key lifecycle. Customer-supplied keys (CSEK) require you to provide the raw key with every API request and Google never stores it. Client-side encryption happens before data reaches Google, shifting all key management to your application.

ul.li: CMEK keys can reside in Cloud KMS (software-backed), Cloud HSM (FIPS 140-2 Level 3 hardware), or Cloud External Key Manager (EKM) for keys held outside Google infrastructure entirely.
CSEK keys are never stored by Google — they must be provided as a Base64-encoded AES-256 key with every read or write request, making key loss equivalent to permanent data loss.
All Cloud Storage data is encrypted at rest by default using Google-managed keys with AES-256; CMEK and CSEK add customer control on top of this baseline encryption.

Cloud Audit Logs record every use of a CMEK key, providing an audit trail for compliance; disabling a CMEK key immediately renders all objects encrypted with it unreadable until the key is re-enabled.

question.title: Cloud Storage Retention Policy
question.scenario: A company must comply with regulations requiring that certain data cannot be deleted for 7 years, even by administrators.
question.question-text: Which Cloud Storage feature prevents object deletion until a specified retention period has passed?

choices.choice: IAM deny policies
Object versioning
Retention policy with bucket lock
Object lifecycle rules

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: A retention policy sets a minimum retention duration on a bucket, and locking the bucket makes that policy permanent and irreversible — even project owners cannot delete objects before the period expires.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Retention policies define a minimum duration that every object in a bucket must be retained. When combined with bucket lock, the retention policy becomes permanent and cannot be removed, shortened, or overridden. This creates immutable storage meeting regulatory compliance requirements like WORM (Write Once Read Many). Even project owners and organization admins cannot delete locked objects before retention expires. IAM deny policies can be changed by sufficiently privileged admins. Object versioning preserves history but does not prevent deletion. Lifecycle rules automate deletion, the opposite of retention.

ul.li: Bucket lock is irreversible — once applied, the retention policy cannot be removed or shortened for the lifetime of the bucket, so thorough testing is essential before locking.
Object holds (event-based and temporary) provide additional per-object protection layered on top of retention policies, useful for litigation holds on specific documents within a retained bucket.

Retention policies prevent object deletion and overwrite but do not prevent reading; locked data remains accessible for the full retention period, satisfying both preservation and access requirements.
Lifecycle Delete rules cannot override a retention policy — if a lifecycle rule tries to delete an object still under retention, the deletion is silently skipped until the retention period expires.

question.title: Storage Selection: Media Rendering
question.scenario: A media company's rendering farm needs shared storage accessible by hundreds of VMs simultaneously for reading input files and writing output.
question.question-text: Which storage solution provides high-performance shared file access for compute-intensive workloads?

choices.choice: Filestore High Scale tier
Cloud Storage
Persistent Disk multi-attach
Local SSD

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Filestore High Scale (Zonal) tier provides high-throughput NFS storage designed for HPC and rendering workloads where hundreds of VMs need simultaneous read-write access to shared files.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Filestore High Scale tier (formerly Zonal) delivers high-throughput NFS storage purpose-built for compute-intensive workloads like media rendering, genomics pipelines, and HPC simulations. It supports simultaneous read-write access from hundreds of clients with throughput scaling into tens of GB/s. Cloud Storage has higher per-operation latency and lacks POSIX semantics needed by rendering software. Persistent Disk multi-attach only supports read-only mode, preventing render workers from writing output. Local SSD is per-VM ephemeral storage with no sharing capability.

ul.li: Filestore High Scale can deliver up to 26 GB/s aggregate throughput, sufficient for rendering farms where hundreds of worker VMs read large texture and geometry files simultaneously.
Persistent Disk multi-attach allows connecting a single disk to up to 10 VMs but in read-only mode only, making it unsuitable for rendering workflows that must write output frames to shared storage.

Higher Filestore capacity provisions higher baseline throughput; for burst-heavy rendering jobs, over-provisioning capacity is a common strategy to ensure sufficient I/O headroom during peak rendering passes.

For rendering farms that stage input from Cloud Storage, a common pattern is to pre-load assets onto Filestore before a render job and copy completed frames back to Cloud Storage for long-term archival.

question.title: Storage Selection: Compliance Archive
question.scenario: A healthcare organization must store patient records for 10 years to meet regulatory requirements. The data is rarely accessed but must be protected against accidental or malicious deletion.
question.question-text: Which Cloud Storage configuration ensures data cannot be deleted before the retention period expires?

choices.choice: Archive storage class with retention policy and bucket lock
Standard storage with object versioning
Nearline storage with lifecycle rules
Coldline storage with IAM deny policies

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: For regulatory compliance requiring guaranteed 10-year retention with deletion protection, combine the lowest-cost storage class with a retention policy locked by bucket lock to make it permanent and irreversible.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: The correct configuration combines Archive storage (lowest cost for rarely accessed data), a retention policy set to the required 10-year duration, and bucket lock to make that policy permanent and irrevocable. Once locked, no user — including project owners and organization admins — can delete objects before the retention period expires, satisfying HIPAA and other healthcare compliance requirements. Standard storage with versioning does not prevent deletion. Nearline with lifecycle rules automates deletion, the opposite of preservation. Coldline with IAM deny policies can be overridden by sufficiently privileged administrators.

ul.li: Bucket lock is a one-time, irreversible operation — once applied, the retention policy cannot be removed, shortened, or modified for the lifetime of the bucket; thorough testing with an unlocked policy is essential first.

Object holds (event-based and temporary) can be layered on top of retention policies for additional protection, useful for placing litigation holds on specific patient records without affecting the entire bucket.

IAM deny policies can restrict deletion permissions but can be modified or removed by organization administrators, so they do not provide the same immutability guarantee as bucket lock for regulatory compliance.

Archive storage class has a 365-day minimum storage duration charge, but for 10-year retention this is irrelevant; the cost savings over Coldline (90-day minimum) or Nearline (30-day minimum) accumulate significantly over a decade.
